summary: When one outcome is rare, accuracy can be high for a model that finds nothing.
headline: 99% accurate and useless
overview: If only 1 case in 100 is positive, a model that always says no is right 99% of the time and finds none of them.
Accuracy hides it. Recall, precision and the precision-recall curve show it.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Drop the positive share to 1% and let the model always say no. Accuracy sits near 99% while recall is zero.

check.question: A fraud model is 99% accurate when 1% of cases are fraud. What should you check next?
options: How many frauds it actually catches
Whether the data is balanced in the test set only

realLife: Fraud, rare diseases and equipment failure are all imbalanced, so accuracy alone is a poor guide.
data: Four thousand cases with a share of truly-yes cases you set. Scores come from the same two bell curves as the metrics lesson. The threshold slider still applies.
maths: ROC AUC does not depend on prevalence, because it compares positives with negatives directly. Precision does depend on it.
code:
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
model = LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced')
average_precision_score(y, p), roc_auc_score(y, p)
